newsitem.title: USA: Dollar falls vs. mark, gains against yen.
newsitem.headline: Dollar falls vs. mark, gains against yen.

text.p: NEW YORK, March 12 - The dollar fell against the German mark Wednesday after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer again objected to strength in the U.S. currency, but it rose against the yen as Japanese interest rates fell.
Speaking after a French-German summit in Lyon, France, Tietmeyer repeated his opposition to further gains in the dollar and stressed that Germany remains interested in a "stable" mark.
The dollar has risen 28 percent against the mark after it hit a post-World War II low of 1.3438 marks on March 8, 1995.
"He's basically trying to say that he believes that the dollar has corrected against the deutschemark," said Mike Malpede, a senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
Traders said the dollar also fell indirectly as a result of the mark's sharp gains against the yen.
The dollar slid further when orders to sell were triggered as the currency tumbled below 1.70 marks.
In late trading, the dollar fetched 1.6928 marks, down from 1.7037 marks late on Tuesday.
But the dollar rose to 122.27 yen from 121.78 yen as the yield on the benchmark 10-year Japanese government bond fell to a record low of 2.295 percent.
Japanese bond yields are much lower than those of Canada, Germany, the United States, Australia and New Zealand.
"So, it encourages capital to flow out of Japan, which weakens the yen (and) helps the dollar," said John Rothfield, an international economist at Nationsbanc.

The dollar erased some gains against the yen and deepened its losses against the mark after the Federal Reserve's "Beige Book" survey of economic conditions indicated the U.S. economy continued to grow with little inflationary pressure.

Fed policy-makers will use this information when they meet on March 25 to consider whether to raise short-term interest rates for the first time in over two years. Higher U.S. rates would make dollar-denominated assets more attractive, and fuel demand for the currency.

"People are reading in the Fed will not raise with these comments and with the Beige Book, but I don't think that's going to be the case," said Mark Gargano, managing director of currency derivatives at First Union National Bank.
"But that is what they're reading into it (and) definitely why they're selling (dollars)," he said.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.4550 Swiss francs from 1.4708 francs on Tuesday.
The British pound fell to $1.5987 from $1.6075.
The dollar fell to Canadian $1.3631 from C$1.3673.
